12.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this shoulder or elbow prosthesis?"
- "Shoulder: is the ball on the **humerus** (anatomic) or on the **glenoid** (reverse)?"
- "Elbow: the radial head alone, the whole hinge, or the humeral end only."

| Implant | Look for | Replaces |
|---|---|---|
| **Hemiarthroplasty** | stem and head, no glenoid part | humeral head only |
| **Anatomic total (aTSA)** | head plus white polyethylene (PE) glenoid | head and glenoid |
| **Reverse total (rTSA)** | ball on glenoid, cup on stem | swaps ball and socket |
| **Resurfacing, stemless** | cap or short anchor | head surface |
| **Radial head prosthesis** | small head on a stem | radial head |
| **Total elbow (TEA)** | humeral and ulnar stems, hinge | whole elbow |
| **Distal humeral hemi (DHH)** | humeral stem with a spool | trochlea and capitellum |

- An aTSA needs a working cuff; a reverse works without one

- Hemiarthroplasty, anatomic total and reverse total on X-ray
- Radial head prosthesis, total elbow and distal humeral hemi

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Head only, head plus socket, socket swapped**

12.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this stem with a ball?"
- "A **shoulder hemiarthroplasty**: humeral stem and metal head; the glenoid is left alone."
- "Today mainly for unfixable fractures and for arthritis with a good glenoid."

### When
- Elderly four-part and head-split fractures, or head arthritis with a healthy glenoid
- Osteonecrosis limited to the head gives the best results
- Failed plate in the elderly: revise to a hemi (Prof Amr Rashwan)

- Failed plate revised to a hemi; tuberosities later absorbed

### The fracture stem
- Its lean upper body takes graft from the head, to help tuberosity healing
- A slot takes the sutures; depth marks on the trial set height

- Fracture stem with its depth marks

### Height and version
| Check (Rockwood) | Target |
|---|---|
| Retroversion | **30°** |
| Head top above greater tuberosity | **5–9 mm** |
| X-ray | "gothic arch" restored |

- Gothic arch: lateral scapular border flows into the medial humeral shaft
- Stem too proud: tuberosity low, cuff tight; too deep: tuberosity high, impingement
- Between head sizes, choose the smaller

### Tuberosities decide the result
| Sutures | Grip | Through |
|---|---|---|
| **Four** | greater tuberosity | posterior cuff |
| **Two** | lesser tuberosity | subscapularis |
| More | vertical hold | shaft drill holes |

- Keep cement out of the tuberosity beds

- Tuberosity healing before early motion; nonunion still in about **18%**

- Tuberosities tied around the stem: photo and drawing
- Fracture hemiarthroplasty one year after surgery

PITFALL — "does a bigger head give more motion?"
- A head too large overstuffs the joint
- Say → "**Overstuffing limits motion and tears the cuff. Match the native head.**"

- Oversized humeral head overstuffing the joint

12.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this shoulder with a white glenoid?"
- "An **anatomic total shoulder**: humeral stem and head, plus a cemented PE glenoid."
- "It needs an **intact rotator cuff**."

### When, and when not
- End-stage arthritis with an intact cuff: osteoarthritis, rheumatoid, osteonecrosis, post-traumatic
- Not with infection, an irreparable cuff tear or a paralysed deltoid

### Humeral side
- Modular stems and heads mix to fit; offset heads match the head centre
- Cobalt-chrome or titanium, porous upper coat; short and stemless designs save bone

| Generation (Handbook) | Design |
|---|---|
| First, 1970s | monoblock |
| Second, 1990s | modular stem and head |
| Third, 2006 on | adjustable head position |
| Stemless | cap on a porous metal bed |

- Short-stem humeral component with a porous upper body
- Modular heads: centred and offset
- Ultrashort stem and stemless implant on X-ray
- Stemless total shoulder with an ingrowth glenoid

### Glenoid side
- Cemented all-PE glenoid is the gold standard; radius 2–4 mm larger than the head

| Glenoid | Pegged | Keeled |
|---|---|---|
| Use | most shoulders | severe bone loss |
| Load | central, even | — |
| Bone removed | less | more |
| Loosening | lower | higher |
| Radiolucent lines, one trial | 15% | **46%** |

- Uncemented metal-backed glenoids failed more; largely dropped

#### Glenoid position
- Posterior wear: eccentric reaming lowers the anterior rim
- Retroversion beyond about **18°** cannot be reamed away → bone graft or augment
- Superior tilt of the glenoid component risks later cuff failure (Campbell)

- Glenoid designs: keeled, pegged and ingrowth-peg
- Metal-backed glenoid in an anatomic total shoulder

### Steps that matter
#### Open and cut
1) Deltopectoral approach; subscapularis cut and tagged
2) Humeral cut with a guide at **30°** retroversion

#### Glenoid
3) Glenoid: guide pin, then reamer
4) Drill peg or keel holes; syringe cement into them

#### Tension and close
5) Head tension: it slides half the glenoid width, then springs back
6) Repair the subscapularis well; its failure means anterior instability

| Tight subscapularis (Campbell) | Gain |
|---|---|
| Z-lengthen by **1 cm** | about **20°** more external rotation |

PITFALL — "can I use an anatomic glenoid with a torn cuff?"
- Torn cuff → head rides up → loads the top of the glenoid
- Say → "**No. It loosens like a rocking horse. A dead cuff needs a reverse.**"

12.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this reverse shoulder?"
- "A **reverse total shoulder**: ball on the glenoid, PE cup on the humeral stem."
- "Its centre of rotation moves down and in, so the **deltoid** lifts the arm."

### Parts (Miller)
| Part | Job |
|---|---|
| **Baseplate** | porous plate on the glenoid |
| Central peg or screw | anchors it in the vault |
| Peripheral screws | lock the baseplate |
| **Glenosphere** | ball on a Morse taper |
| Humeral stem | cemented or press-fit |
| **PE cup** (liner) | socket; thickness sets tension |

- Reverse prosthesis: glenosphere, liner, humeral tray and stem

### How it works
- No cuff → the deltoid pulls the head up instead of rotating it
- Fixed fulcrum, centre medial and distal → deltoid tightens, gains lever arm, lifts alone
- Grammont introduced the modern reverse, early 1990s

- Biomechanical theory: the medialised centre of rotation
- No cuff: head escapes; reverse: deltoid lever restored

| Design | Grammont | Lateralised |
|---|---|---|
| Centre of rotation | at glenoid face | lateral to it |
| Neck-shaft angle | **155°** | often 135° |
| Notching | more | less |
| External rotation | weak | better |

- Grammont and lateralised reverse prostheses on X-ray
- Glenosphere lateralisation and inferior overhang

### Indications
- Main indication: a **non-functioning cuff** — cuff tear arthropathy, pseudoparalysis
- Elderly three- and four-part fractures, nonunion, tuberosity malunion
- A failed arthroplasty with a deficient cuff

#### Irreparable cuff tear
- Irreparable tear: retracted beyond the glenoid, no tension-free repair (Nagah)
- Nagah lists reverse among ten options, after spacer and tendon transfer
- Hamada stage 3: acromion acetabularised; only a reverse helps from then on (Prof Maged Samy)

- Re-torn cuff, acromiohumeral distance 4 mm, pseudoparalysis

| Cost in Egypt (Prof Amr Rashwan) | EGP |
|---|---|
| Reverse | about **75,000** |
| Hemi | about **20,000** |

### Operative points
- Always cut the biceps: it hurts and has no role
- Subscapularis cut, tagged, repaired through bone at the end

#### Bone cuts
- Humeral cut just above the bicipital groove; conical reamer for the stem
- Baseplate low and tilted down: see 12.5

#### Tension and stability
- Overlong deltoid risks acromial fracture; mild joint gapping is acceptable
- Subscapularis repair aids stability in Grammont designs, less in lateralised

### Needs
- An intact axillary nerve, a working deltoid and enough glenoid bone
- An absent or fatty teres minor gives poorer results
- No infraspinatus or teres minor → add latissimus dorsi transfer for external rotation (Prof Maged Samy)

#### Survival
- Survival over **90%** at ten years

### In fractures
- Tuberosity healing is not essential → earlier active motion (Rockwood)
- Still tie the tuberosities, for rotation; deltoid tension sets stem depth

- Reverse for a three-part fracture; tuberosity reduced and healed

- Worn glenoid: augmented baseplate or bone graft
- Augmented baseplate in a worn glenoid

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Cuff dead, bone broken, implant failed → reverse**

PITFALL — "hemi or reverse for an elderly four-part fracture?"
- A hemi depends on tuberosity healing; a reverse does not
- Say → "**Reverse. Two meta-analyses found it superior to hemi in the elderly.**"

12.05.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "name this shoulder instrument"
- "Humeral side: canal reamer, **cutting guide**, broach, trial head."
- "Glenoid side: guide pin, **glenoid reamer**, drill guide, baseplate impactor."

### Humeral side (Campbell)
#### Canal
1) Open the canal with a burr at the cuff footprint
2) Hand reamers, never power, until they bite cortex
- Hold the arm loosely while reaming → no spiral shaft fracture

#### Cut
3) **Cutting guide** referenced on the forearm, pinned in retroversion
4) Oscillating saw cuts the head
- The resected head is the template for head size

#### Broach and trial
5) **Broaches** of rising size, kept in the same retroversion
6) Trial stem and trial head; check height and tension

- Humeral head cutting guide in place
- Extramedullary cutting guide set to a chosen inclination
- Reaming canal and glenoid, then baseplate and glenosphere
- Sizing disc, trial and final humeral component

### Glenoid side
1) See all four glenoid rims; remove the labrum
2) Centring guide places the **guide pin**

#### Ream and fix
3) Cannulated **glenoid reamer** runs over the pin
4) aTSA: peg or keel drill guide, trial, then cement

### Reverse extras
| Reverse step, in order | Rule |
|---|---|
| Baseplate low (lower edge) | flush with the inferior glenoid rim |
| Guide pin | about **10°** inferior tilt (Rockwood) |
| Screws, into the pillars | coracoid base, scapular spine, inferior pillar |
| Then the glenosphere | tapped onto the Morse taper |

- Trial liners grow until stable in extension and both rotations (Prof Maged Samy)

- Guide pin, then the glenoid reamer over it
- Baseplate screws, then the glenosphere
- Trial liner, then the definitive PE cup

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Ream, cut, broach, trial — pin, ream, plate, ball**

12.06.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this small mushroom-shaped implant?"
- "A **radial head prosthesis**: a metal head on a short stem in the radial neck."
- "It restores the lateral strut when the head cannot be fixed."

### When
- Comminuted head that cannot be fixed, with elbow instability
- Mason III with an MCL injury or a dislocation (Handbook)
- Mason IV: fix or replace; in Essex-Lopresti it stops proximal radial migration

#### Restraint and view
- The MCL is the primary valgus restraint; the radial head is secondary
- Greenspan (radial head–capitellum) view separates the head from the coronoid (Handbook)

- Fracture-dislocation before and after a radial head implant

### Designs
| Choice | Options |
|---|---|
| Pieces | monoblock or modular |
| Head | fixed (monopolar) or bipolar |
| Stem | cemented, press-fit, smooth loose |
| Material | metal; silicone abandoned |

- Silicone caused synovitis and did not stop migration
- No design has proved best; press-fit stems loosen in a third or more
- Smooth stem: 1 mm under the rasp, so the head self-centres (Rockwood)

- Bipolar and monopolar radial head prostheses
- Loose-fit monobloc and cemented bipolar implants on X-ray

### Insertion (Campbell)
1) Kocher interval if the LCL is torn; EDC split if intact
2) Incise the annular ligament; cut the neck at the fracture

#### Prepare and fit
3) Rasp the canal; cut flat for the collar
4) Trial, then fluoroscopy through motion
5) Final implant; LUCL back to its isometric point

#### Safety and motion
- Forearm pronated, no retractor in front of the neck → PIN safe
- Heavy retraction or an oversized press-fit stem can split the neck
- No associated injury → active motion at once

- Annular ligament opened for an end-on view of the canal
- Trial radial head and its check in theatre

### Sizing
- Rebuild the fragments on the back table to judge the size
- Diameter: the native head's small diameter; between sizes, the smaller
- Never size from the capitellar gap: a torn LCL hides overlength

#### Height
- Implant top level with the lateral coronoid edge

- Lateral coronoid edge marks the implant height
- Check tracking in flexion: no edge binding

PITFALL — "how much too long is too long?"
- Over **2 mm** of lengthening raises capitellar pressure
- Say → "**Overstuffing gives pain, stiffness and capitellar wear. Look for a lateral ulnohumeral gap.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Rebuild it, size it small, sit it at the coronoid**

12.07.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this elbow hinge?"
- "A **linked semiconstrained total elbow** (Coonrad-Morrey): humeral and ulnar stems joined by a pin."
- "Its 'sloppy hinge' has a little play, which spares the cement."

### Three levels of constraint (Campbell)
| Type | Link | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| Constrained | rigid metal hinge | abandoned: it loosened |
| **Semiconstrained (linked)** | pin, PE bushings, laxity | no ligaments needed |
| **Unconstrained (unlinked)** | none | ligaments, capsule, bone |
| Convertible | either | decided in theatre |

- Linked hinge: about **7°** of side-to-side and rotary play
- Anterior humeral flange, with graft behind it, resists torque

| Result | Semiconstrained | Unconstrained |
|---|---|---|
| Ten-year retention | **92%** | 76% |
| Lost to | — | loosening, instability |
| True dislocation | — | under **5%** (Campbell) |

- Instability overall: **9–10%**

- Fractures: linked TEA preferred; the broken condyles may be excised

- Coonrad-Morrey and Nexel linked elbows, exploded
- Coonrad-Morrey prosthesis in three sizes
- Four unlinked total elbow designs
- Sorbie-Questor and Latitude: anatomic humeral implants

### When
| TEA | Who |
|---|---|
| Yes | unfixable distal humeral fracture, over **65** |
| Classic candidate | rheumatoid elbow |
| Also | post-traumatic arthritis, bad ankylosis |
| Caution | under **50**: very high complication rate |
| Not | prior sepsis, neuropathic joint, heavy use |

- Shoulder and same-side elbow both need replacing: do the more painful first (Campbell)
- Cement columns must overlap, or leave a long gap

### Insertion (Campbell)
#### Approach
1) Posterior incision; transpose the ulnar nerve
2) Triceps-on approach preferred: no triceps rupture

#### Humerus
3) Remove the mid-trochlea; open the canal at the olecranon fossa roof
4) Alignment stem, then a cutting block resting on the capitellum

#### Ulna and trials
5) Burr into the ulna through the olecranon tip; rasps
6) Trials in full extension; cement restrictors and a cement gun

#### Cement and link
7) Ulnar component first, then humeral with graft behind the flange
8) Axis pin and split locking ring: a click confirms it

#### Axis checks
- Flange flush with the olecranon fossa → axis at the right height
- Flexion axis: **14°** internal to the flat posterior humeral cortex (Rockwood)

- Coonrad-Morrey steps: nerve, humerus, ulna
- Coonrad-Morrey steps: cement, link, triceps repair
- Distal humeral broach, then trials in extension

#### After surgery
- Triceps-off: no active extension for three months; triceps-on: move once the wound heals

### For life
- No single lift over **5 kg** (Stone 2022)
- No repeated lifting over **1 kg**

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Linked needs nothing; unlinked needs everything**

PITFALL — "is the Coonrad-Morrey a constrained hinge?"
- It is linked, but not rigid
- Say → "**Semiconstrained: a sloppy hinge. Fully constrained hinges loosened and were dropped.**"

| Lost to | — | loosening, instability |
| True dislocation | — | under **5%** (Campbell) |

- Instability overall: **9–10%**

- Fractures: linked TEA preferred; the broken condyles may be excised

- Coonrad-Morrey and Nexel linked elbows, exploded
- Coonrad-Morrey prosthesis in three sizes
- Four unlinked total elbow designs
- Sorbie-Questor and Latitude: anatomic humeral implants

12.07.2.b:
| TEA | Who |
|---|---|
| Yes | unfixable distal humeral fracture, over **65** |
| Classic candidate | rheumatoid elbow |
| Also | post-traumatic arthritis, bad ankylosis |
| Caution | under **50**: very high complication rate |
| Not | prior sepsis, neuropathic joint, heavy use |

- Shoulder and same-side elbow both need replacing: do the more painful first (Campbell)
- Cement columns must overlap, or leave a long gap

12.07.3.b:
#### Approach
1) Posterior incision; transpose the ulnar nerve
2) Triceps-on approach preferred: no triceps rupture

#### Humerus
3) Remove the mid-trochlea; open the canal at the olecranon fossa roof
4) Alignment stem, then a cutting block resting on the capitellum

#### Ulna and trials
5) Burr into the ulna through the olecranon tip; rasps
6) Trials in full extension; cement restrictors and a cement gun

#### Cement and link
7) Ulnar component first, then humeral with graft behind the flange
8) Axis pin and split locking ring: a click confirms it

#### Axis checks
- Flange flush with the olecranon fossa → axis at the right height
- Flexion axis: **14°** internal to the flat posterior humeral cortex (Rockwood)

- Coonrad-Morrey steps: nerve, humerus, ulna
- Coonrad-Morrey steps: cement, link, triceps repair
- Distal humeral broach, then trials in extension

#### After surgery
- Triceps-off: no active extension for three months; triceps-on: move once the wound heals

12.07.4.b:
- No single lift over **5 kg** (Stone 2022)
- No repeated lifting over **1 kg**

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Linked needs nothing; unlinked needs everything**

PITFALL — "is the Coonrad-Morrey a constrained hinge?"
- It is linked, but not rigid
- Say → "**Semiconstrained: a sloppy hinge. Fully constrained hinges loosened and were dropped.**"

12.08.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this humeral stem with a spool?"
- "A **distal humeral hemiarthroplasty**: a stem whose spool replaces trochlea and capitellum."
- "No ulnar part and no PE; the patient's own ligaments hold it."

- Latitude EV: the only licensed DHH; modular and cemented (Stone 2022)
- Its cannulated spool takes ligament sutures; converts to a TEA, stem left in

### Needs
| Must have | Why |
|---|---|
| No arthritis of native surfaces | they bear the load |
| Intact coronoid | stability |
| Columns intact or fixable | carry the epicondyles |
| Ligaments intact or repairable | they stabilise |

- Radial head intact too (Rockwood)

### Plus and minus
- No PE wear, fewer lifting limits; but opposite cartilage wears, instability likelier
- Revision in about **4%**, all to a TEA

- Latitude stem, pin and spool
- Trial hemiarthroplasty in the lateral para-olecranon window
- Hemiarthroplasty with a medial column plate
- Medial epicondyle K-wire into the cement mantle

PITFALL — "between two sizes: bigger or smaller?"
- Radial head and DHH spool go opposite ways
- Say → "**Radial head: smaller. DHH spool: larger, to spread the load.**"

12.09.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what has gone wrong here?"
- "aTSA: glenoid loosening. Reverse: scapular notching. Radial head: overstuffing or a loose stem."
- "Total elbow: loosening, bushing wear, infection."

### Anatomic total shoulder
- Glenoid loosening is the commonest failure: almost half by **10** years
- A loose glenoid shifts, or shows a full lucent line of **1.5 mm**
- Humeral lucency usually means infection

#### Instability
- Anterior instability: subscapularis failure, the most common pattern (Miller)
- Small head → instability; big head → stiffness
- Inferior instability after fracture hemi: humerus left short → weak deltoid

- Lucent lines progressing to gross glenoid loosening
- Undersized head leaving the joint unstable

### Reverse shoulder
- **Notching**: the PE cup hits the scapular neck in adduction

| Nerot grade | Notch |
|---|---|
| 0 | none |
| 1 | small |
| 2 | with condensation, stable |
| 3 | evolutive, reaches the inferior screw |
| 4 | glenoid loosening |

- Most notches stop at grade 2
- Prevent it: low baseplate, inferior tilt, lateral ball, varus stem

#### Fracture, dislocation, infection
- Acromial fracture is the most worrying complication: overlong deltoid, osteoporosis
- Dislocation is anterior, in extension and external rotation
- Infection: *Cutibacterium acnes*; hold cultures **10–14** days

- Nerot grades of scapular notching
- Grade 1 notch, and a notch progressing to grade 3
- Acromial fracture and grade 4 notching after reverse
- Loose baseplate with a broken screw

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Low, tilted, lateral — no notch**

### Elbow
- Radial head overstuffing: see the 12.6 pitfall
- Smooth stem: thin stable lucency is normal; ingrowth stem: progressive lucency means loosening

#### Total elbow
| TEA failure | Fact |
|---|---|
| Loosening | mostly humeral |
| Bushing wear | young, male, post-traumatic, highly active |
| Commonest complications | ulnar neuritis, triceps insufficiency |
| Infection | about **3%** of primary operations |

- TEA for acute trauma, UK registry: revision in **6%** (Stone 2022)
- That is at **8** years, mostly for aseptic loosening or infection

- Loose press-fit radial head stem
- Bipolar radial head disassembled after a new fall
